text: Good morning, everyone. I'm Jimmy Bierman, chair of our transportation committee. Welcome to the Board of Supervisors Transportation Committee meeting of September 22nd, 2026. We'll start the meeting as we always do with a question of whether or not anybody has changes to the summary of the June 16th meeting minutes. And as we always do, absolutely nobody has changes, so we're going to get right to it. We've got a full meeting today. We've got first an update from the VDOT Northern Virginia District Mega Projects team, and then an update on our active transportation

projects audit. And with that, I'm just going to jump right into it and turn it over to Bill Cutler to introduce his team. Thank you. Thank you very much, Supervisor Beerman. I'm Bill Cutler. I'm the district engineer, the leader of VDOT here in Northern Virginia District.

Thanks for having us today. I'm with Krishna Paturi, who is our Northern Virginia District Megaprojects Director, and is going to walk through a slide presentation on two large projects on the interstate that we are conceptualizing right now.

I'll turn it over to you, Krishna. Thank you. All right. Good morning, everyone. I'm Krishna Paturi. I'm the Megaprojects Director at VDOT. I started with VDOT about three months back. I'm happy to hear to give you an update on two studies we are working on currently.

As you all know, with the opening of Project NEXT, the 495 Northern Extension, we now have 97 miles of express lanes. And express lanes continue to be a key solution in managing congestion and unreliability in our region.

So we are, I'll go over both the studies we are currently working on, the 95 bidirectional project and the south side express lanes project. All right, the first one, the 95 bi-directional, as you know, currently the 95 express lanes are reversible and operate only in the peak travel direction, and they start at Springfield Interchange and go all the way to exit 133, which is Route 17 in Stafford County.

VDOT and Transurban, we continue to explore feasibility of adding bi-directional traffic for approximately 45 miles. This starts from Springfield Interchange all the way to Spotsylvania Parkway and Fredericksburg area, and the proposed concept will build three express lanes in each direction in the northern section, which is from Springfield Interchange to Prince William Parkway, and then it will transition from the three express lanes in each direction to express lanes in each direction from Prince William Parkway all the way to Spotsylvania Parkway in South

in Spotsylvania County, sorry. The next slide you see here is a stick diagram where we are looking at. This is focused on Fairfax County. What you see there in the purple color is the express lanes. What you see in gray is all the general purpose lanes and the access through general purpose lanes. The two purple lines indicate the three express lanes that will be in Fairfax County from Occoquan all the way to Franconia Springfield Parkway.

And that will connect back to the reversible system. And then we have a northbound express lanes running for the last two miles north of Franconia Springfield Parkway to Springfield Interchange. Where we are currently, we just entered into a development framework agreement with Transurban to develop this project.

That was signed at the end of June, and we started working on this project. VDOT is heading up the environmental and traffic studies, and then Transurban is working closely with VDOT to develop the concept. We expect to have public information meetings in 2027 with a public hearing schedule.

Our goal is to have public hearing in 2028. Once the project is decided to be feasible and we get the necessary approvals from Federal Highway, we expect the project to move into commercial close and financial close in the year 2029.

Following that, TU will submit a binding proposal to VDOT in 2029, and the construction would begin approximately in the year 2030. We continue our coordination with the agencies and the county staff to develop design details on this.

And this is my last slide on the bidirectional. We just started working on this project. We are laying out the concepts. We see most of the project footprint is within the existing right-of-way. There are some areas where we will have to take some right-of-way takes for different purposes, some of the management ponds or things like that.

But we are in a very early stages of the project where all the conceptual geometric details are being ironed out. With that, I'll pause here for a second before we move on to the next study we are working on, which is the 495 south side.

I think it's good since we've got two studies to offer up the opportunity for questions right now on the first, which is the bidirectional express lane study. Sorry, Mr. Chairman, yes. Not really a question. I just want to thank you for the presentation. This is the first time we've seen a tentative timeline. This was probably the biggest mistake ever made in Virginia's interstate system. And I, for one, am proud to be saying that at the time I was saying this is a huge mistake to do this section of 95 the way it is. And if you look at it out there every single day, you can see evidence of exactly why it was a big mistake.

So I really appreciate all the work that VDOT, Secretary of Transportation, and others are doing to advance this and give us some real dates. I think one of the points that you mentioned, which can't be mentioned enough, was another thing that, you know, I know I said and others said, and I'm not an engineer, which is it seems like this can fit largely in the existing right-of-way.

And now to get a confirmation that largely this can fit in the existing right-of-way changes the dynamics of this project significantly. and hopefully through the course of the public meetings and discussion on this will also help advance it as quickly as possible because obviously there are some environmental impacts anytime you do road work but in this particular case you know a lot of the right-of-way is already out there it's underutilized and people are sitting in traffic looking at traffic in the other direction free-flowing and wondering why they don't have an option and it's very frustrating

So I am very grateful and thankful that you have a timeline here. I would also add that, you know, largely this segment of 95 benefits people outside of Fairfax County for the large part. But it harms everyone in Fairfax County that this traffic is sitting dead stopped, at least in one direction most of the time.

And so while a lot of this is not physically within Fairfax County, it does have an impact on our residents and the environment in Fairfax County. And my hope is that these dates stick pretty well and that you find this project to be tremendously popular with the public.

I believe it will be. And I just wanted to express not only my support for this project, but my gratefulness to you all for advancing it and providing us some dates and some hope that we can finally fix this section of interstate and put it on an equitable level with every other piece of interstate in Northern Virginia.

Thank you. Supervisor Alcorn and then Supervisor Stork. Yeah, just very quickly. This is – I totally concur with everything that the chairman just said. And my only question is, this has been through at least the study part, is part, has been approved by the TPB, correct?

And it's in there. Is there anything pending right now for this? Yeah, so I can talk to that. So we studied 11-mile section of the project in previous years. That portion of the project is currently in the TPB.

But now that we have expanded the project all the way to Spotsylvania Park. So the additional part. The additional part needs to be added to. Okay, thank you. Because I knew part of it was in. I just didn't understand that much. Thank you. Thank you. TPB means Transportation Planning Board. Sorry, just clarification for those watching at home, all six of you.

Supervisor Stork. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. And I'm obviously pleased to see Lorton Road access in there. think it's huge, a major mistake when it's really done. And what I don't know, and I'm smiling as I say that, is anybody who goes down that way during rush hour knows how horrible really all the traffic is. And it's really more of a function of 123. But the amount of people that jump off 95 at that point in time and how they clog the rest of the roads around there, I mean, that is one of the

major and most sensitive issues that I have as a supervisor because it literally brings to a stop and a crawl 123, Lorton Road, I mean all the furnace road, really all the back roads that potentially route one, etc. So I don't know how that gets addressed and I realize I'm saying something that probably everybody would shake their head and go yeah that's a problem but I think it has to be part of how do we engineer this to minimize people jumping off and clogging up local roads because they're either unwilling to to be on 95 or the express lanes so i i just

want to weigh in on that and and urge that be part of the engineering look of that and i would also ask that there be uh engagement deep engagement with the south county federation and the south county community because those folks live it every day and and and you all have i know have heard generally about the traffic lights on Lorton Road and the timing of those. And I don't know that you could ever get them 100% right, but because of the Amtrak and the different other I-95 and all the other kind of turns and changes there that it's, we're also looking for something

there. And then a final piece of that, which I think could make a difference in that whole intersection, and that's ultimately what you're looking at is how do you kind of fix the Lorton Road intersection is to pay for and support the pain for a continuous right turn from Lorton Road onto Silverbrook Road. Jerry Connolly, Congressman Connolly got a study, got money for a study to kind of look at that. And I think some of it may be done, but I think the cost of the study, et cetera, et cetera, has gone up. So I don't know that that was ever complete, but that

would also, I think, do a lot to improve traffic flow. And then my maybe final point is something that is very important to me. I know very important to a number of my constituents, the Potomac Heritage National Trail. Are you familiar with the Potomac Heritage National Trail?

Okay. My colleagues, I don't know how many of them are, but it's a trail that runs literally from Maryland all through northern Virginia, mostly down to Alexandria. And over time, We're trying to make it a little bit more enjoyable to hike, not along railroads, et cetera. And so we're looking at a piece, particularly from the VRE station that goes over to Laurel Hill and Liberty, the former Lorton maximum security prison, et cetera, looking for how we can support that and having the trails go underneath not only CSX tracks, the new VPRA tracks that are being built, as well as the I-95 tracks.

So ultimately the trail connections there and then ultimately across the Occoquan River are a big deal. So I'm looking for ways, and I know you're going to hear it maybe even more loudly from others in the community about how do we build that into what's getting built.

Much like what was done in I-66, looking for ways for pedestrians and bicyclists to literally cross the Occoquan River, To really do that now is almost impossible. I mean, theoretically, you'd use Route 1, but it's not safe, and there's really no trail or access point there.

So those are core, critical elements that I think have to be part of the planning. And I would say for mine and the community support, we'll have to be part of it because they're so central and so important to the future of traffic access and trail and pedestrian access.

And we all know that we're going to see more and more and more and more and more electric bikes and scooters as a major mode of transportation. And to not have people be able to cross the Occoquan without some easy use of that would also be as short-sighted as having this be a one-way directional railway versus the bi-directional that we're planning now.

So thank you. Thank you, Supervisor Stork. any other questions on this topic seeing and hearing none i stole that from chairman mckay we'll go to the next one which is the south side express lane study thank you all right our next study we are actively working on is the the 495 south side express lanes project um as you all know we kicked off this project back in 2022 there has been several public meetings for this project The project itself is 11-mile extension of express lanes from Springfield Interchange

all the way into Maryland, Maryland 210. There have been more than 10 concepts that were studied, and then we whittled it down to two concepts, which is taking one express lane in each direction or two express lanes in each direction.

And finally, we presented two express lane concepts back in 2025. So the corridor faces significant regional mobility challenges, there's a lot of recurring traffic congestion, unreliable travel times, and limited travel choices including no HOV or no reliable transit service, and also limited bicycle and pedestrian access for the community.

So this has been coordinated with multiple agencies, Fairfax County, City of Alexandria, Prince George's County and others so just to take you back to our previous proposal a little bit the previous proposal took advance took that space which was available on Woodrow Wilson Bridge and that was that was used to accommodate the two express lanes on Woodrow Wilson Bridge based on some

extensive feedback we received from the region that that place was the the ask from the region was to preserve that space for a future metro and because of that in fall 2025 the project was not added to the regional long-range transportation plan effectively pausing that study so we kind of lost about 12 to 15 months we we we went back to the drawing board and with the new administration

Starting early 2026, we started looking at other ways how we can address the feedback we received from the public and all the localities. What you see on this slide here is the new concept, so we broke it down into three.
The one on the top is the existing configuration on Woodrovers and Bridge. What you see in the middle is the new concept, and then at the bottom is how the new concept would address a future metro.

So the way we did that is we took the local lanes, which are three local lanes on the outside, and converted them into four general purpose lanes. And then we used the through lanes in the middle, which are two through lanes, into express lanes.
So by doing that, we still leave that space in the middle, which is 18 feet on both sides, for a future metro. And this has been a major change from what the concept we had before.

Most of the geometry remains the same on the Virginia side. It's how this lane configuration changes in Maryland is something we are working on. But at the crux of it, this is the one key element of the design that is being revised.
And I want to point out that for this to happen, it requires some sacrifices. To accommodate those four lanes on the outside, we need to reduce the shoulders and use that space.

Otherwise, there is no way to leave that space in the median for metro and still be able to accommodate six lanes. So the coordination is underway with Maryland, SHA. We have been having constant meetings with SHA to kind of take this concept further down.

And because there will be other changes at interchange 295 and 210. So we are working through those concepts right now. but this is the major change with the new concept. Where we are, we plan to present the revised concept to public and stakeholders later this year, and we are targeting early 2027 for inclusion of the project into the TPB.

And one of the key points I want to make here is it's so important for the project to be included in the TPB because that will give us the opportunity to extend the studies we are already doing. We currently gathered more traffic information to understand the impact of this project on side streets.

That is really important for us to make sure that whatever detrimental effect the project is inducing on side streets are clearly addressed. So we went back, gathered more traffic information, and we are actively working on new traffic analysis. But the important thing is to get that regional consensus and include the project in TPB so that we can continue our studies and gather more information.

As you all know, the project is very unique. We are working towards finding a solution which is workable for both Virginia and Maryland. It is complicated because the needs on both sides of the river are different.

So we continue our discussions with the stakeholders. We are having meaningful conversations with several locality partners and we hope to continue that engagement throughout this year and early part of next year.

And I did just want to add one more thing. Thank you so much. Last week at the Commonwealth Transportation Board, or CTB, Deputy Secretary Carter Hutchison presented this project. It's on the web, our VDOT CTB website.

You can take a look at that. Included in his presentation was Virginia committing an annual transit funding amount of at least $15 million per year. That is a floor, and the intent is for that to grow.

And part of how that could grow is through the agreements with should we go the private concessionaire route. there is opportunity for growth there. But at least a floor has been placed in terms of the Commonwealth's commitment to transit funding. That was a very important addition that the Secretary and the administration made in being responsive to our region, including Maryland and Prince George's County, who have expressed interest in that. So if I could summarize some of the three

main changes in our concept that was not supported by the region previously includes the preservation of the space for the metro rail, as was illustrated in Krishna's slide, the transit payment floor, the transit floor, I should say, of $15 million a year, the intention that that would be even bigger than that, but at least it's a starting point, and then also the commitment to be looking at the side street traffic. And that would be a written commitment that the Commonwealth would

make as well. And that would be to the benefit of our local governments in Virginia, as well as our local governments in Maryland. Thank you. Thank you. With that, I will turn it over to questions starting with Chairman McKay. Yeah. So first, before I ask my question, I think your response to the concerns that came up at CTB over a sustained period of time are outstanding. I mean, honestly there's a limit to what you can do here with the existing bridge and frankly I think this is better than a lot of us thought in terms of getting commitments and certainly address the

issues that I have heard most significantly. I will comment on the side street piece just briefly because Supervisor Stork in the last presentation was presenting exactly what my concern has been from day one that these lanes are not extended, which is they are a major reason the side streets have problems. Because when the interstate isn't working right, where does the traffic go? It diverts and it finds ways around. That doesn't mean that there aren't impacts of the project, but I've just always been consistent on this point that it seems like concerns over the side

streets are being driven by the project when in fact a lot of the existing conditions on the side streets are being driven by the lack of infrastructure in this section of the beltway that exists everywhere else in Virginia. And the fact that there's no transit benefit to the people who live in this corridor still to me is a leading equity issue why this is important.

So I'm a strong supporter of this. I appreciate what you've done to make it more palatable to the region. And I'm hopeful that CTB will see that progress as well. The technical question that I have, and I know this was explained to me, but I'm not sure many people in the public understand it. The way the segments are on page eight, especially where the divider walls are, there's structural reasons for that. And so I know I asked the question of could the dedicated metro portion of the right of way, could that be used currently as a bus only lane,

which would be great, but for the fact that there's some technical reasons why that can't happen, and then also why you can't adjust to be able to provide for emergency shoulder space on the bridge right now.

So can you explain the technical reasons why those things would be difficult? Yeah, so thank you very much for the question. And the space in the middle, which is a wide shoulder, geometrically, we can put a lane there.

The challenge comes in at both the interchanges, how we take those buses across the express lanes or across the GP lanes back to wherever we're connecting back to. So that would be the challenge, I would say, from a feasibility standpoint.

And then I will touch upon the incident management, when we put four lanes on the outside with narrowed shoulders, there is a concern about what happens during the incident, we thought about that internally too, and one of the things we have successfully implemented is having the project pay for a tow truck sitting on both sides of the bridge, which will be available instantaneously for any incident that can be cleared.

That happens on 66 currently, and we expect to include that as a term in the term sheet for the project. Yeah, I think that's important because one incident that clogs that up can offset the entire benefits of the infrastructure advancement that you're pushing for.

And, you know, and I appreciate the bus comment. I will say that if this was built today and was existing, there would be a lot of frustration for people that might potentially be sitting in traffic looking at a space for another lane that is just sitting there that they can't use.

But I also think in order to move the project and advance the project moving forward, preserving that for future Metro Rail is a necessity. And so it will be frustrating, but it is, in my mind, a necessity to be able to preserve that. I would just say on the bus piece, understanding the technical issues with that, I do think it's something we continue to look at as this project advances, because it's one thing to see space there that nobody can use.

It's another to see that space being used by transit that could be converted into rail in the future. And I know that there's a lot of reasons why that is a very difficult thing to accomplish. But I hope we don't stop looking at it, at least in creative ways, potentially to do that, because there is going to be a perception issue here down the road.

We don't know where the traffic volumes are going to be by the time this gets built. We don't know what the embrace of transit is going to be. There's a lot of unknowns at this point. But what we all know sitting here today is anytime there's a piece of infrastructure that can't be accessed by people while they're sitting in traffic, there's a political pressure point.

And so I just want us to just keep looking at that dedicated use for metro and keeping that in here for the reasons that we need to be able to secure CTB support, but also continue to think about some bus options there.

Sure. Thank you very much for the comment. I just wanted to point out, and also the express lanes, transit travels for free. That is probably one of the reasons why we did not look at exclusive bus rapid transit lanes. But we can definitely take that back and see what we can do about it.

Yeah, I mean, to me, that's an important reason to do the express lanes, period, is to be able to get the buses and them to be able to use them. Here you have this very unique situation, though, that doesn't exist anywhere else where you might be able to have your cake and eat it, too, and that's why I just want to make sure we don't foreclose on that opportunity before it's researched heavily.

Sure. Thank you. I saw Supervisor – I'm going to go in the order of hands I saw. So Supervisor Palchik, Supervisor Alcorn, Supervisor Lusk, Supervisor Stork, and Supervisor Herity. And if you can remember the order for me, I would appreciate that. That was great.

Supervisor Palchik, please. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. Thank you so much, Mr. Peturi and Mr. Cutler. I think my comments were mainly in line with the chairman as looking at, number one, appreciate that we've been able to preserve the future rail. And the question of both, I'm not an engineer, but the question of both shoulders and programming in the interim phase, I think, whether it's, you know, additional support while we're at it from whoever will be planning, owning this project, if it can't be done structurally,

to do programmatically, because we do know whenever there's a stoppage, and my husband drives this every day, so he knows how difficult it can be when there is a stoppage, that we're able to go quickly and address that. So I do think that's critical to be included in here, especially, you know, as we know the workforce that's going to be living on both sides of the river going to existing places, including the future sphere on the Maryland side, is I think the connectivity is a number one thing we've heard from our regional economic development partners and

leaders, and so anything that improves that connectivity, right, I think we'll have a return on investment as well as the transportation. Because to me, that's a big part of this, is the ROI to our regional economic work in addition to the transportation piece, right, is when we get stuck, the region gets stuck.

So I appreciate the flexibility and would say let's continue to study ways in the interim to be able to address, you know, issues that arise and have our engineers and planners really take a deep look at that and include that in our contracts.

And secondly, you know, I appreciate because although we have that bus on the northbound lanes without the express lanes, it gets stuck in traffic. So very much appreciate that here, anything we can do. Number one, there are express lanes, but number two, if there are other ways to be flexible to understand, I've seen quite a few motorcycles going across here, right, going to work and back.

And so I appreciate this. I do think we have to bring it to modern times, and I feel like this is a step forward in that direction. Thank you. And then finally, I was going to ask if we have data on side street traffic where we have built express lanes, because this is something I want to get as much through traffic on, you know, the highways and off our streets as possible.

It seems intuitively to do that. And so I just want to make sure we're looking at data when we're making those decisions. Yeah, yeah. Thank you very much for those comments. And from a connectivity standpoint, we are actively engaging with SHA and their needs on the Prince George's County side.

So that is being, we are looking at multiple access points. We are looking at ways to make that flow better between Route 1 and 295. That's ongoing. And just in terms of the side street traffic, for this corridor, we have collected new traffic data.

So we have more current traffic data that we will be using in our analysis expanse outside. Just looking at 495, we go at least two intersections outside to look at what impact 495 will have on the side streets.

So that is ongoing. We have done this on all our express lanes projects. That is something we look closely and to the point that was made earlier. I think the important part is if the bedway flows better, there will be less impact on the side streets.

Our effort is going to be so much focused on making the 495 corridor, give more travel choices, to be working actively with other transit routes that we can add because once the infrastructure is in place, there will be more opportunities to run more buses, move more people, right?

The only way we can resolve the congestion is by moving more people and not with the space available. These are highly congested urban corridors. So we are looking at all those, and we are using express lanes as a tool to kind of solve the situation.

I appreciate it. And to do that, my only question would be is if you've been able to go back and look at your original projections for the existing lanes and how accurate were we, you know, looking at the side street traffic. I haven't seen that. I don't know if you have that and can share it with us, just so we are looking at facts and not reactions, right, to potential problems.

Yeah, we can share that. Thank you. Appreciate it. Thank you, Supervisor Palachuk. Supervisor Alcorn. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. So just to build on the comments, I very much appreciate this new approach that's being put forward. I think it is going to be received more favorably by a number of the stakeholders in the region. This is definitely helpful.
I did want to note one thing that Chairman McKay was talking about in terms of use of that right-of-way. With our newly adopted regional bus guidelines, we now have definitions.

We have actually different terms that we use. We used to just say BRT, and BRT was BRT, and it's like lots of different terms. Now we have different categories of BRT. BRT, bus priority, bus priority. So I would encourage you as you look at this project to think a little bit how those types of BRT might fit in here, not just for Fairfax County and Alexandria, but frankly for PG County too.

And there could be potentially some future project that comes out of this. And then just to build on, there has been a lot of history here. I want to really underscore how, to me anyway, in my conversations that I've had with folks on this side of the river and on the other side of the river, how common some of the concerns and issues are across Fairfax County, City of Alexandria, and PG County.
And I know we, as a board, about a year ago, sent a letter to VDOT about a number of different intersections and roads that were needing to be looked at. What's the impact?

Not just the impact for this project, but if the project happens, but also what if the project doesn't happen to build on what Chairman McKay was saying. I think looking at sort of the common issues that we face along with Alexandria, along with PG County, is a good way to look at this because, you know, frankly, we need them on board.

You know, we need to get our partners across the river to step up and work with us on this. So this is a great movement in that direction. And again, I just want to underscore that some of the concerns I've heard from them are very similar to the concerns that we have here as well.

And working together, I'm confident we can work through these and solve this. So thank you. Thank you, Supervisor Alcorn. Again, for the folks watching at home, Supervisor Alcorn is all about the acronyms today. BRT is Bus Rapid Transit. And I do know that our friends across the river prefer when you call it Prince George's County.

With that, I will turn it over to Supervisor Lusk. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. I'll sort of dovetail on some of the points that Supervisor Alcorn made, and I'll just make the point first that I really appreciate the new concept.

Just love the addition of the metro lanes. I think that makes a lot of sense. The thing that I'm still struggling with is I remember when we were kind of rolling this out to our partners across the Potomac River and their vehement opposition to this project was a surprise to me. So I'm going to be honest, I thought there were some benefits even with the previous iteration and recognize that that wasn't, at least from their public points and

positions at the time, that wasn't necessarily the case. So I guess the question I have here is, in terms of our conversations with Maryland, and I guess we've had some, I'm assuming, what has been their position with regard to the new concept? I'm assuming that you're feeling that we're getting to a better place, but just trying to understand what has been your assessment of where they are in light of this new concept. Thank you for that comment and question. I think

From their perspective, the space in the median for Metro, that's a big ask, and this concept addresses that. The second thing I would say is a transit commitment, and that is something, like Bill said, Virginia is ready to commit to a floor, a transit payment, and that would be applied within the corridor.

And that is something I think is in the positive direction. So that addresses some of their concerns. And we still have to, do we have a yes today from them? No. But we are working towards and having those meaningful conversations.

Okay. So I guess the expectation is that we will get to a yes, which I'm hoping that that is the case. But I'm also recognizing that there were some significant challenges from before. So just wanted to maybe get a sense of how you see this, but it sounds like from your perspective here, we're making positive steps and we're moving in the right direction.

That is correct because of the new concept is the first time we are presenting it to them and they have to kind of, we're giving them that opportunity to review the new concept and see what that means and how that addresses their previous concerns.

Yeah, so there's yet to have that back-and-forth dialogue with them. But it's good. It feel like where we are today We feel like we are moving in a positive direction. Okay. Well, I'll acknowledge and say I appreciate the work that you're doing and we certainly are very supportive of it We certainly want to get to a place where we can get Maryland and our colleagues across the stomach River to a yes So thank you. Thank you Supervisor Lusk, Supervisor Stork, and then Supervisor Herity. Thank you, mr.

chairman and uh thank you all very i'm going to go into the chairman's comments particularly about the quote-unquote unused lane i know that that's been a sensitive issue and i i am a thousand percent in support of making sure we have a lane for metro whenever we get to that point but i i am probably equally a thousand percent against not using that lane in some way um until such time i mean i want to guarantee if you will so that nobody can ever say we won't yeah put metro because we already have this other thing there.

But I also, I know I am going to get verbally abused, and who knows where it goes after that, if people see an unused lane on that bridge. I mean, there already is now, but if these changes are made and there's that space on the bridge, I just, I'm telling you, it's not going to be worth all the abuse that we will all take.

I know, I mean, I'm sure VDOT will get more than their fair share of it. So I am not supportive of just leaving that open or unused. So I know there has to be some guarantee. I've had this conversation with the state representatives about this, and some of them aren't as, I guess, supportive as I am of making sure that that lane gets used because their fear, and it's not unreasonable, their fear is that whenever the day comes that we want to run MetroCross there, that somehow or other it might not happen.
